newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Treasuries end higher ahead of FOMC meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Treasuries end higher ahead of FOMC meeting.

text.p: The U.S. Treasury coupon sector closed higher at the end of a dull Monday session, with key players remaining on the sidelines on the eve of a Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
Volume was thin as many market participants took the day off to celebrate the Jewish holiday of Yom Kippur.
The bill sector came under some pressure, reflecting the market's almost evenly divided expectations about the decision the 12-member policy-setting arm of the Federal Reserve will take on Tuesday.
In a Reuter survey, 17 of 30 economists said the Fed is likely to raise the 5.25-percent federal funds rate on Tuesday. All but one of the 17 firms expected a 25-point hike.
Five firms -- Aubrey Lanston, DLJ Securities, MFR Inc., Lehman, and Standard and Poor's -- are expecting a 25-point hike in both funds rate and 5.0-percent discount rates.
Barclays de Zoete Wedd Government Securities is the only firm expecting a 50-point increase in both benchmark rates.
"Our view basically is that wage pressure is building and needs to be addressed," said BZW chief economist Steve Ricchiutto.
Ricchiutto said there is no sign that "wage pressures haven't done anything but mount."

The latest Fed's Beige Book -- prepared by the 12 Fed banks for discussion at the FOMC meeting -- showed U.S. labor markets getting increasingly tight, with none of the 12 Fed districts reporting any ebbing in wage pressures.

Ricchiutto said his call for a 50-point hike was tied to the view a preemptive Fed policy "makes sense" in the current economic environment, as it did during the February 1994-February 1995 tightening cycle -- "the last time the Fed was pushed in this situation."
Ricchiutto said the Fed is currently facing the opposite situation it did in 1994 when the prices of commodities were soaring -- but wages were stagnant.
The BZW chief economist said the market's reaction to any Fed decision will largely depend on the wording of the accompanying communique rather than on the move itself.
"The next move in the market will depend on what type of statement will follow the rate announcement, whether it's a one off move or not," Ricchiutto said.
Traders said the front end has priced not more than a 25-point funds rate hike.
A dual move -- and even more so a 50-point move -- is bound to hurt the front end, but could lift the long end on heightened Fed credibility and lower inflation expectations.
Senior economist Astrid Adolfson at MCM MoneyWatch agreed the market's reaction to the FOMC decision "will depend more on the wording of the announcement."
"If it says the economy is stronger than expected and we can take away the insurance policy, not only could the long end rally, but the front end could move in sync," she said.
The 6-3/4 percent 30-year benchmark Treasury bond ended up 8/32 at 96-19/32 to yield 7.02 percent.
MCM MoneyWatch does not expect a Fed move on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, a Reuter report saying the Fed is about to peg its policy to a core Consumer Price Index range between zero and two percent contributed to the gains late in the session.
At the close, the three- and six-month T-bill rates were up two basis points at 5.16 percent and 5.30 percent, respectively, and the year bill down one at 5.52 percent.
The two-year note was unchanged at 99-25/32 and 6.24 percent, the five-year note up 3/32 at 98-30/32 and 6.60 percent and the 10-year note up 5/32 at 101-9/32 and 6.82 percent. -- 212-859-1676
